questions.text: Compare New Urbanism and CIAM's Athens Charter on their approach to mixed-use development. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Both advocate for separating residential from commercial uses, emphasizing distinct zoning to prevent land use conflicts
CIAM advocated separation; New Urbanism advocates mixing—they are opposite philosophies
Both emphasize transit connectivity and public transportation, aiming to reduce reliance on private vehicles
New Urbanism evolved as a refinement of CIAM principles, incorporating lessons learned from past urban planning practices

rationale.a: CIAM advocates separation (correct). New Urbanism advocates MIXING (opposite).
rationale.b: CIAM (1933) advocated zoning into four separate functional zones—the doctrine that caused urban dysfunction. New Urbanism (1980s+) is an explicit reaction AGAINST CIAM's separation, advocating mixed-use neighborhoods where residential, retail, services, and offices coexist. They represent opposite values.
rationale.c: Transit was not central to CIAM's Athens Charter doctrine (it was written pre-modern transit). New Urbanism incorporates transit integration.
rationale.d: New Urbanism emerged as a critique and rejection of CIAM's legacy, not a refinement of it.
rationale.correct: CIAM (1933) advocated zoning into four separate functional zones—the doctrine that caused urban dysfunction. New Urbanism (1980s+) is an explicit reaction AGAINST CIAM's separation, advocating mixed-use neighborhoods where residential, retail, services, and offices coexist. They represent opposite values.
rationale.takeaway: CIAM = separation (problems it caused: dead downtowns, isolation). New Urbanism = mixing (solution to CIAM's problems). Opposite philosophies.

questions.text: Carlos Moreno's 15-Minute City concept requires residents to access all daily needs—work, food, health, education, culture, and parks—within what time frame?

options.text: 5 minutes by foot
10 minutes by transit
15 minutes by foot or bike
20 minutes by any mode of transport

rationale.a: 5 minutes is New Urbanism's neighborhood radius, not the 15-minute city.
rationale.b: Moreno's concept prioritizes active transport (foot/bike), not transit time.
rationale.c: Moreno (2020) defined the 15-Minute City as all daily needs accessible within 15 minutes by foot or bike. This extends the New Urbanism neighborhood concept to a more functionally complete daily-life radius while maintaining active transport priority.
rationale.d: 20 minutes is not part of Moreno's framework, and the concept allows 'any mode' (it specifies foot or bike).
rationale.correct: Moreno (2020) defined the 15-Minute City as all daily needs accessible within 15 minutes by foot or bike. This extends the New Urbanism neighborhood concept to a more functionally complete daily-life radius while maintaining active transport priority.
rationale.takeaway: 15-Minute City = 15 min foot/bike access to all daily needs. Moreno, 2020. Newer than New Urbanism; more inclusive functionality.

questions.text: Ebenezer Howard's Garden City concept targets a self-contained community of how many people?

options.text: 32,000 people (maximum)
100,000 people
500,000+ people (metropolitan)

rationale.a: Too small—10,000–20,000 would not support the range of services Howard envisioned.
rationale.b: Howard's Garden City (1898) targeted 30,000–60,000 people—large enough for diverse services and employment, small enough to preserve community identity and green space. This specific range is fundamental to Howard's vision.
rationale.c: ERR-PLAN-023 error—students often round up to 100,000. This is incorrect. Howard was explicit that massive size defeats the garden city purpose.
rationale.d: 500,000+ would be a metropolis, not a self-contained garden community.
rationale.takeaway: Garden City = 30,000–60,000. Exact range matters. Howard's vision: Goldilocks community size.

questions.text: A city implements policies promoting infill development, walkability, mixed-income housing, and environmental conservation while discouraging sprawl. This policy framework aligns most closely with which approach?

options.text: Garden City model—new town construction
Smart Growth principles—urban-scale anti-sprawl policy
Growth Pole Theory—concentrated investment and spread effects
CIAM zoning—functional separation strategy

rationale.a: Garden City is about building new self-contained towns, not infill in existing cities.
rationale.b: Smart Growth is a comprehensive policy approach (1990s–present) featuring compact infill development, walkability, mixed uses, transit, mixed housing, and environmental protection—all anti-sprawl principles. This is broader than New Urbanism (which focuses on neighborhood design) and is explicitly policy-oriented.
rationale.c: Growth Pole Theory focuses on concentrated sectoral investment generating spread effects—not anti-sprawl policy per se.
rationale.d: CIAM zoning is the problem Smart Growth reacts against.
rationale.correct: Smart Growth is a comprehensive policy approach (1990s–present) featuring compact infill development, walkability, mixed uses, transit, mixed housing, and environmental protection—all anti-sprawl principles. This is broader than New Urbanism (which focuses on neighborhood design) and is explicitly policy-oriented.
rationale.takeaway: Smart Growth = urban policy framework emphasizing infill, walkability, transit, mixed use, environmental conservation, and anti-sprawl. Broader than New Urbanism.

questions.text: A planner proposes a development near an MRT station with higher density, mixed retail-residential uses, and reduced parking. This design approach aligns most closely with which contemporary urban model?

options.text: Garden City model—self-sufficient community planning with green belts and limited population sizes to prevent urban sprawl
New Urbanism—walkable neighborhood design that emphasizes mixed-use development and sustainable communities
Transit-Oriented Development—density and mixed use around transit stations
CIAM separation—functional zoning efficiency that separates residential, commercial, and industrial areas to optimize urban planning

rationale.a: Garden City is about self-contained new towns, not station-area intensification in existing metro areas.
rationale.b: New Urbanism includes walkability and mixed use but is not specifically transit-anchored. TOD takes New Urbanism principles and organizes them around stations.
rationale.c: This is a textbook TOD project: anchored to transit (MRT station), higher density, mixed use (retail-residential), reduced parking (transit-dependent). New Urbanism also values walkability and mixed use, but TOD is specifically defined by transit-station anchoring.
rationale.d: CIAM's separation doctrine is the opposite of this mixed-use approach.
rationale.correct: This is a textbook TOD project: anchored to transit (MRT station), higher density, mixed use (retail-residential), reduced parking (transit-dependent). New Urbanism also values walkability and mixed use, but TOD is specifically defined by transit-station anchoring.
rationale.takeaway: Station-area, density, mixed use, reduced parking = TOD. Remember: TOD = transit-oriented design with 400–800m catchment.

questions.text: François Perroux's Growth Pole Theory proposes that concentrated investment in a strategic economic sector or location generates what to surrounding regions?

options.text: Immediate reduction in regional inequality, leading to balanced economic development
Spillover effects and agglomeration benefits ('spread effects')
Automatic equal distribution of wealth across regions, ensuring uniform prosperity
Reduction in urban density at the pole location, allowing for more sustainable growth

rationale.a: Growth poles may increase inequality initially; spread effects are gradual and not automatic.
rationale.b: Perroux (1955) theorized that concentrated investment in a growth pole generates 'spread effects'—agglomeration benefits, supply-chain linkages, labor market effects, and infrastructure spillovers that stimulate development in surrounding regions. Clark development corridor policy reflects growth pole thinking.
rationale.c: Growth poles concentrate investment, not distribute equally.
rationale.d: Growth poles increase density at the location; reduction of density is not the mechanism.
rationale.correct: Perroux (1955) theorized that concentrated investment in a growth pole generates 'spread effects'—agglomeration benefits, supply-chain linkages, labor market effects, and infrastructure spillovers that stimulate development in surrounding regions. Clark development corridor policy reflects growth pole thinking.
rationale.takeaway: Growth Pole = concentrated investment → spread effects → regional agglomeration. Perroux, 1955. Applied to Clark corridor.

questions.text: What is the 5-minute walk radius in New Urbanism, measured in meters?

options.text: 200 meters
400 meters
800 meters
1000 meters

rationale.a: Too close—200m is roughly 2.5-minute walk. Not sufficient for New Urbanism's intended service coverage.
rationale.b: New Urbanism (Duany, Plater-Zyberk, Calthorpe) defines the 5-minute walk as 400 meters at a comfortable pedestrian pace (~4–5 km/h). All daily needs—groceries, services, parks, transit—should be within this radius.
rationale.c: ERR-PLAN-025 error—800m is the UPPER BOUND of TOD (Transit-Oriented Development), not New Urbanism. New Urbanism = 400m; TOD = 400–800m.
rationale.correct: New Urbanism (Duany, Plater-Zyberk, Calthorpe) defines the 5-minute walk as 400 meters at a comfortable pedestrian pace (~4–5 km/h). All daily needs—groceries, services, parks, transit—should be within this radius.
rationale.takeaway: New Urbanism 5-min walk = 400m. TOD catchment = 400–800m. Don't confuse them.

questions.text: The CIAM Athens Charter (1933) advocated for cities organized into four separate functional zones: living, working, recreation, and transportation. What is the primary critique of this approach?

options.text: It created too much density in urban cores, leading to overcrowding and infrastructure strain
It resulted in dead downtown areas, isolated neighborhoods, and car dependency
It did not allocate enough green space, reducing urban biodiversity and recreational areas
It concentrated all government functions in one zone, limiting accessibility and service distribution

rationale.a: CIAM created low-density zones, not too much density. The problem was scattered, car-dependent development.
rationale.b: CIAM's separation of functions was meant to rationalize cities but led to dysfunction: dead downtowns (no residents), isolated residential areas (no services), and automobile dependency (distances between zones forced car travel). Contemporary models like New Urbanism explicitly reject this zoning doctrine.
rationale.c: CIAM advocated 'towers in a park'—actually generous green space. But the critique is about separation, not insufficient green.
rationale.d: Government concentration in one zone is a minor issue; the main problem is functional separation creating urban dysfunction.
rationale.correct: CIAM's separation of functions was meant to rationalize cities but led to dysfunction: dead downtowns (no residents), isolated residential areas (no services), and automobile dependency (distances between zones forced car travel). Contemporary models like New Urbanism explicitly reject this zoning doctrine.
rationale.takeaway: CIAM = separation = dysfunction. Contemporary models = mixing = vitality. Don't confuse CIAM principles with New Urbanism (opposite values).

questions.text: Which contemporary urban model specifically anchors development around mass transit stations with a walkable catchment of 400–800 meters?

options.text: Garden City, which emphasizes green spaces and self-contained communities but does not focus on transit proximity
New Urbanism, which promotes walkable neighborhoods and mixed-use development but not necessarily centered on transit stations
Transit-Oriented Development (TOD)
15-Minute City, which aims for all essential services to be within a 15-minute walk or bike ride, not specifically transit-focused

rationale.a: Garden City predates modern transit theory (1898) and is about self-sufficient new towns, not transit-anchored development.
rationale.b: New Urbanism uses 400m for a 5-minute walk but is not specifically transit-anchored. TOD expands this to 400–800m for station-area development.
rationale.c: Transit-Oriented Development (TOD, Calthorpe et al., 1990s–present) is explicitly designed around mass transit stations. The 400–800m catchment represents the walkable area around a station. Higher density, mixed use, and reduced parking are hallmarks of TOD.
rationale.d: 15-Minute City (Moreno, 2020) is about accessing all daily needs within 15 minutes by foot/bike, not specifically transit-station focused.
rationale.correct: Transit-Oriented Development (TOD, Calthorpe et al., 1990s–present) is explicitly designed around mass transit stations. The 400–800m catchment represents the walkable area around a station. Higher density, mixed use, and reduced parking are hallmarks of TOD.
rationale.takeaway: TOD = transit stations as development anchors. 400–800m catchment. Applicable to MRT-adjacent development in Metro Manila.

questions.text: If a neighborhood provides all daily needs (work, food, health, education, culture, parks) within a 5-minute walk (400m), it meets New Urbanism standards but falls short of which contemporary model that requires 15 minutes of active transport access?

options.text: Transit-Oriented Development—which requires station proximity and integration with public transport networks.
Garden City—which requires 30,000–60,000 population and a balance of green spaces and urban areas.
15-Minute City—which extends accessible daily needs to a 15-minute radius
Smart Growth—which prioritizes regional density policy and sustainable land use planning.

rationale.a: TOD requires 400–800m from transit stations—overlaps with both New Urbanism and 15-Minute City but is not the direct comparison.
rationale.b: Garden City requires 30,000–60,000 population scale, not a time-distance metric.
rationale.c: New Urbanism defines a complete neighborhood at 400m (5 min walk). Moreno's 15-Minute City (2020) expands this to 15 minutes on foot/bike—accommodating a broader geography and more specialized services (major health, education, employment centers) beyond the immediate neighborhood.
rationale.d: Smart Growth is policy framework, not a specific time-distance standard.
rationale.correct: New Urbanism defines a complete neighborhood at 400m (5 min walk). Moreno's 15-Minute City (2020) expands this to 15 minutes on foot/bike—accommodating a broader geography and more specialized services (major health, education, employment centers) beyond the immediate neighborhood.
rationale.takeaway: New Urbanism = 400m/5-min walk. 15-Minute City = 15-min walk/bike. Moreno extends the neighborhood concept to a larger, more functionally complete radius.
